strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant limitation of Reservoir Computing: sequential processing and memory footprint of dense high-dimensional reservoirs, by porting the diagonal complex linear recurrence and associative-scan parallelization strategy from LRU/SSMs into the RC paradigm.

Provides theoretical grounding: a clean necessary-and-sufficient condition for the Echo State Property under a diagonal complex transition matrix (Theorem 4.1), and a proof that any linear ESN can be represented by an equivalent diagonal complex ParalESN via diagonalization (Proposition 4.2), leading to a universality corollary for the model class.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning memory-capacity tasks, chaotic/real-world forecasting, UEA/UCR classification, and 1-D pixel-level classification (sMNIST/psMNIST), together with a computational complexity analysis (Appendix B) and comparisons against other structured RC variants (SCR, Structured RC) and fully-trainable models (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba).

Reports concrete and consistent efficiency gains (training time, energy consumption, CO2 emissions) alongside accuracy, and demonstrates scaling to reservoir sizes where traditional dense ESNs run out of memory (Fig. 2), which is a practically meaningful contribution.

Includes hyperparameter sensitivity analysis and critical-difference statistical comparison plots, improving transparency of the empirical claims, and appendices with substantial detail on datasets and experimental protocol that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an application of existing ideas (LRU's diagonal complex linear recurrence and parallel scan) to the RC setting; the main theoretical argument (Proposition 4.2) is essentially the same diagonalization argument already used to justify LRU, limiting originality.

Accuracy improvements over traditional RC are inconsistent across benchmarks: ParalESN (deep) is sometimes worse than ESN (deep) (e.g., SinMem20, ctXOR10, several ETT forecasting metrics), which somewhat undercuts the claim that the method 'matches' or improves upon traditional RC predictive accuracy uniformly.

Evaluation is restricted to relatively short/small-scale sequence benchmarks (classic RC memory/forecasting tasks, MNIST-scale classification); no evaluation on longer-sequence or larger-scale tasks (e.g., Long Range Arena) that are standard for assessing parallelizable SSM-style architectures and where the claimed logarithmic-time scaling advantage would be most consequential.

Comparisons to fully-trainable baselines (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba) use fixed, relatively small parameter budgets and limited training epochs (100 with early stopping), raising questions about whether these baselines are fully optimized, which could affect the fairness of the performance/efficiency trade-off claims.

The mixing layer (random convolutional kernel) is a somewhat ad hoc design choice with limited justification beyond a sensitivity sweep; its role in compensating for the loss of cross-unit interaction from the diagonal transition matrix is not rigorously analyzed, and no ablation isolates its individual contribution to overall performance.

No explicit statement about code/artifact release, which combined with the many hyperparameters and per-layer configurations reported (Table 8) creates a moderate reproducibility burden despite the detailed appendix.

strengths: The paper is clearly motivated and tackles a well-known pain point of Reservoir Computing: the sequential nature of reservoir updates and the memory cost of dense high-dimensional transition matrices.

The theoretical analysis is self-contained: a spectral-radius condition for the Echo State Property of the complex diagonal recurrence is proven, and an equivalence result shows that any linear ESN (dense transition matrix) can be re-expressed as a complex diagonal ParalESN via diagonalization, which is then used to argue preservation of universality in the fading-memory filter class.

The experimental evaluation is broad, spanning memory-capacity tasks, chaotic/real-world forecasting, UEA/UCR classification, and pixel-level sMNIST/psMNIST, and includes comparisons not just to traditional (deep) ESNs but also to other structured RC methods (SCR, Structured RC) and fully-trainable sequence models (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba).

Efficiency claims are substantiated with concrete wall-clock time, energy, and CO2 measurements (via CodeCarbon) rather than asymptotic complexity alone, and a complexity table (Appendix B) formalizes the time/space trade-offs relative to competing structured RC approaches.
Critical-difference/statistical significance analysis (Wilcoxon test) is used to rank models, which is a more rigorous practice than simple average comparison.
weaknesses: The core architectural novelty is limited: the method is essentially a direct transplant of the LRU's diagonal complex linear recurrence (Orvieto et al., 2023) into the RC paradigm, with reservoir weights frozen. The paper's own framing ("By combining... RC with the linear recurrence from LRU") acknowledges this is primarily a recombination of existing ingredients rather than a new mechanism.

The theoretical contributions are relatively shallow extensions of known facts: the ESP condition for a diagonal matrix is an elementary consequence of the standard spectral-radius argument for ESNs, and the equivalence proof (Proposition 4.2) is a direct application of matrix diagonalizability; the universality corollary largely restates existing results (Grigoryeva & Ortega, 2018a;b) rather than establishing genuinely new theory.

Empirical gains over deep ESN baselines are inconsistent: in several memory-based and forecasting tables (e.g., Table 1 ctXOR10, Table 2 Lz25/MG84/N10/N30/ETTh1), ESN (deep) matches or outperforms ParalESN (shallow), and Fig. 3 shows no statistically significant difference between ParalESN (deep) and ESN (deep), undercutting the claim that the proposed architecture is clearly superior rather than merely more efficient.

On the headline MNIST comparisons against fully-trainable models, ParalESN underperforms LRU/Mamba/Transformer by ~1-2 accuracy points (96.2-97.2% vs 98.4-98.5%), which is non-trivial for these well-studied benchmarks; the "competitive" framing somewhat overstates parity.

The claimed logarithmic time complexity relies on an idealized assumption of Θ(T/log T) parallel processors for the associative scan, which is unlikely to hold in practice on real hardware for large T; the empirical speed comparisons use only modest reservoir sizes (128 units) and the practical scaling behavior under realistic hardware constraints is not fully explored.

The model introduces a substantial number of additional hyperparameters (ρmin/max, θmin/max per layer, mixing kernel size/scale, concat flag, etc.) requiring extensive Bayesian search (up to 24h per configuration per task), which raises reproducibility and practical-efficiency concerns that are not reconciled with the paper's efficiency narrative.

The ad hoc design of the mixing function (1D convolution + tanh applied to the real part) lacks strong justification or ablation beyond a hyperparameter-sensitivity sweep on a single task (NARMA10); its necessity and alternatives are not rigorously explored.
No explicit Limitations section is provided in the main text, and reproducibility details (e.g., code release for the proposed method itself, as opposed to baseline repos) are not clearly stated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: RC's two main scalability bottlenecks (sequential processing and memory footprint of dense reservoirs) are precisely identified and directly addressed by porting diagonal, complex-valued linear recurrence (inspired by LRU/SSMs) into the untrained RC paradigm, which is a sensible and underexplored bridge between RC and state-space/SSM literature.

Solid theoretical contribution: a clean necessary-and-sufficient ESP condition for diagonal complex recurrences (Theorem 4.1), and a diagonalization-based equivalence argument (Proposition 4.2) showing ParalESN can represent arbitrary linear-recurrence ESNs, leading to a universality corollary consistent with known fading-memory results. Proofs are included and appear technically correct for the generic case.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning memory-capacity tasks, synthetic and real-world forecasting (ETT datasets), UEA/UCR time-series classification, and 1-D pixel-level MNIST/permuted-MNIST classification, together with a careful complexity analysis (Appendix B) and hyperparameter sensitivity study (Appendix G).

Strong, consistent efficiency gains are demonstrated: order-of-magnitude reductions in training time, energy consumption, and CO2 emissions relative to traditional ESNs, with logarithmic (vs linear) scaling in sequence length and the ability to scale reservoirs far beyond what dense ESNs can fit in memory.

Useful additional baselines against other structured RC approaches (SCR, Structured RC) and against fully-trainable sequence models (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba), situating ParalESN's accuracy/efficiency trade-off within a broad competitive landscape.
Thorough reporting of experimental methodology, dataset statistics, and hyperparameter search ranges in the appendix, which aids reproducibility even though no code link is provided in the main text.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the core technical device (diagonal complex linear recurrence enabling associative-scan parallelization) is adopted essentially unchanged from LRU/S4/S5; the main novelty is its application within the untrained RC paradigm plus the accompanying ESP/universality analysis, which is a useful but incremental combination rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The diagonalization-based equivalence proof (Proposition 4.2) implicitly assumes Wh is diagonalizable; the paper only hand-waves non-diagonalizable (defective) matrices via 'arbitrarily small perturbations,' leaving the equivalence claim technically approximate rather than exact in that edge case, without further discussion of implications.

Statistical significance results (Fig. 3, critical-difference plot) show no significant difference between ParalESN (deep) and ESN (deep) in predictive performance; the paper's accuracy improvements are therefore mainly significant for the shallow variant, and the central performance claims for the strongest (deep) configuration rest primarily on efficiency rather than accuracy gains.

It is not fully disentangled whether accuracy improvements originate from the complex diagonal/parallel recurrence itself or from confounding factors such as different effective reservoir dynamics/initialization (e.g., complex eigenvalue sampling), since depth alone (already known from DeepESN) explains a large share of the gains for both ESN and ParalESN.

Complex-valued states double the storage per unit relative to real-valued entries, and this nuance is not clearly reconciled with the memory-savings claims in the complexity analysis (Table 5), which could overstate the practical memory advantage.

Baseline fully-trainable models (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba) are relatively small and trained for at most 100 epochs with early stopping to control compute, which may understate their best achievable accuracy and thus bias the performance/efficiency comparison in ParalESN's favor.

No explicit statement of code release/availability is made in the main text, which, despite detailed hyperparameter tables, leaves some reproducibility risk given the complexity of the architecture (diagonal reservoir + ring-topology input matrices + convolutional mixer + multi-layer variants).
